claim: RTP1 and RTP2 are single transmembrane proteins strongly and exclusively expressed in the peripheral olfactory organs.
source: RTP1 (Receptor Transporting Protein 1) and RTP2 (Receptor Transporting Protein 2), both single transmembrane proteins strongly and exclusively expressed in the peripheral olfactory organs (Lu et al., 2003; Saito et al., 2004; Zhuang and Matsunami, 2008; Gimelbrant et al., 1999), greatly enhance the trafficking of ORs to the cell surface of heterologous cells.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Lu et al., 2003; Saito et al., 2004; Zhuang and Matsunami, 2008; Gimelbrant et al., 1999).

claim: RTP1 and RTP2 greatly enhance the trafficking of ORs to the cell surface of heterologous cells.
source: RTP1 (Receptor Transporting Protein 1) and RTP2 (Receptor Transporting Protein 2), both single transmembrane proteins strongly and exclusively expressed in the peripheral olfactory organs (Lu et al., 2003; Saito et al., 2004; Zhuang and Matsunami, 2008; Gimelbrant et al., 1999), greatly enhance the trafficking of ORs to the cell surface of heterologous cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Lu et al., 2003; Saito et al., 2004; Zhuang and Matsunami, 2008; Gimelbrant et al., 1999).

claim: The mouse genome encodes over one thousand intact OR genes.
source: The mouse genome encodes over one thousand intact OR genes (Niimura et al., 2014), which are expressed in a singular and monoallelic fashion in each olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) (Shykind et al., 2004; Chess et al., 1994; Serizawa et al., 2000; Malnic et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Niimura et al., 2014.

claim: ORs are expressed in a singular and monoallelic fashion in each olfactory sensory neuron.
source: The mouse genome encodes over one thousand intact OR genes (Niimura et al., 2014), which are expressed in a singular and monoallelic fashion in each olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) (Shykind et al., 2004; Chess et al., 1994; Serizawa et al., 2000; Malnic et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Shykind et al., 2004; Chess et al., 1994; Serizawa et al., 2000; Malnic et al., 1999).

claim: OSNs express different ORs with dramatically varying probabilities.
source: Each OR is not chosen at random; rather, OSNs express different ORs with dramatically varying probabilities (Khan et al., 2011; Ibarra-Soria et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Khan et al., 2011 and Ibarra-Soria et al., 2014.

claim: Mature OSN axons expressing the same OR project to the olfactory bulb to converge onto specific glomeruli.
source: Mature OSN axons expressing the same OR project to the olfactory bulb (OB) to converge onto specific glomeruli (Mombaerts et al., 1996; Ressler et al., 1994; Vassar et al., 1994; Hayar et al., 2004; Aungst et al., 2003; Gire et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Mombaerts et al., 1996; Ressler et al., 1994; Vassar et al., 1994; Hayar et al., 2004; Aungst et al., 2003; Gire et al., 2012).

claim: When β2AR is expressed instead of an OR, the β2AR-expressing OSNs target their axons to the OB and form glomeruli.
source: When the β2 Adrenergic Receptor (β2AR) is expressed instead of an OR, the β2AR –expressing OSNs target their axons to the OB and form glomeruli (Feinstein et al., 2004a, 2004b; Omura et al., 2014; Nakashima et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations (Feinstein et al., 2004a, 2004b; Omura et al., 2014; Nakashima et al., 2013).

claim: The development of the peripheral olfactory system is dependent on functional GPCRs.
source: Hence, the development of the peripheral olfactory system is dependent on functional GPCRs.
evidence: Inferred from the preceding statement about β2AR-expressing OSNs forming glomeruli.

claim: Heterozygous crosses of Rtp1(+/-);Rtp2(+/-) mice gave rise to wild-type, heterozygous and homozygous adults in roughly 1:2:1 ratio.
source: Heterozygous crosses gave rise to wild-type, heterozygous and homozygous adults in roughly 1:2:1 ratio (Rtp1(+/+);Rtp2(+/+) 19, Rtp1(+/−);Rtp2(+/−) 34, Rtp1(−/−);Rtp2(−/−) 15, n = 10 mating pairs), suggesting no embryonic or postnatal lethality.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from breeding experiments (n = 10 mating pairs).

claim: RTP1,2DKO mice show no embryonic or postnatal lethality.
source: Heterozygous crosses gave rise to wild-type, heterozygous and homozygous adults in roughly 1:2:1 ratio (Rtp1(+/+);Rtp2(+/+) 19, Rtp1(+/−);Rtp2(+/−) 34, Rtp1(−/−);Rtp2(−/−) 15, n = 10 mating pairs), suggesting no embryonic or postnatal lethality.
evidence: Inferred from the 1:2:1 Mendelian ratio observed in breeding experiments.

claim: RTP1,2DKO mice do not express RTP1 and RTP2 transcripts.
source: We validated the absence of RTP1 and RTP2 transcripts in RTP1,2DKO by performing RNA in situ hybridization (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In RTP1,2DKO;M71-IRES-tauGFP OE, GFP staining was observed in the dendrites of Olfr151 positive OSNs.
source: In the RTP1,2DKO;M71-IRES-tauGFP OE, GFP staining was observed in the dendrites of Olfr151 positive OSNs (Figure 1D), indicating that the morphology of their OSNs remains unchanged.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The morphology of Olfr151 positive OSNs remains unchanged in RTP1,2DKO mice.
source: In the RTP1,2DKO;M71-IRES-tauGFP OE, GFP staining was observed in the dendrites of Olfr151 positive OSNs (Figure 1D), indicating that the morphology of their OSNs remains unchanged.
evidence: Inferred from GFP staining in dendrites shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Immunostaining against Olfr151 was restricted to the cell body in RTP1,2DKO mice.
source: In contrast, immunostaining against Olfr151 (Barnea et al., 2004) was restricted to the cell body, indicating these OSNs are unable to traffic the OR to the dendrite (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: RTP1,2DKO OSNs are unable to traffic Olfr151 to the dendrite.
source: In contrast, immunostaining against Olfr151 (Barnea et al., 2004) was restricted to the cell body, indicating these OSNs are unable to traffic the OR to the dendrite (Figure 1D).
evidence: Inferred from the restriction of Olfr151 staining to the cell body in Figure 1D.

claim: RTP1 and RTP2 are essential for OR trafficking.
source: Altogether, the data suggest that RTP1 and RTP2 are essential for OR trafficking.
evidence: Inferred from the OR trafficking defects observed in RTP1,2DKO mice.

claim: The thickness of the OE is significantly reduced in RTP1,2DKO mice.
source: Upon examination of the OE, we found that its thickness was significantly reduced in RTP1,2DKO mice. (p=0.02 paired student t test) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (p=0.02) and data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RTP1,2DKO mice showed an average of 22% reduction in OMP positive area when compared to wild-type.
source: We measured the area occupied by RNA in situ hybridization signal against OMP and found that mice showed an average of 22% reduction in RTP1,2DKO when compared to the wild-type (p<0.0001, paired student t test, wild-type mean area 71% ± 5 (SD), RTP1, 2DKO mean area 49% ± 4 (SD)) (Figure 2C, See methods for details).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of OMP staining with statistical significance (p<0.0001) shown in Figure 2C.

claim: RTP1,2DKO showed a significant reduction in OMP expression at 1 day and 21 days but not at 6 months.
source: Comparison of the OMP positive layer from wild-type and RTP1,2DKO OE collected at 1-day-old, 21-day-old and 6-month-old mice showed a significant reduction in OMP expression at 1 day and 21 days (p=0.0003, Mann Whitney U test, p=0.0003, Mann Whitney U test) but not at 6 months (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis at different time points shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ACIII expression showed a 17% decrease in the area occupied by staining in 21 day old RTP1,2DKO OE.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis of expression of adenylate cyclase 3 (ACIII), a signaling molecule expressed in mature OSNs (Wei et al., 1998; Wong et al., 2000; Col et al., 2007) showed a 17% decrease in the area occupied by the staining in 21 day old RTP1,2DKO OE (p=0.0001, Mann Whitney U test, wild-type mean area 44% ± 9 (SD), RTP1,2DKO mean area 27%, ± 3 (SD)) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunohistochemical analysis with statistical significance (p=0.0001) shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A significant difference in ACIII expression was observed at 1 day old but not at 6 months.
source: Consistent with OMP expression, we observed a significant difference in ACIII expression at 1 day old (p=0.0079, Mann Whitney U test) but not at 6 months (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis at different time points shown in Figure 2E.

claim: GAP43 positive area shows a 7% increase in 21-day-old RTP1,2DKO.
source: GAP43 is a marker for immature olfactory neurons in the OE (Meiri et al., 1988; Verhaagen et al., 1990; Treloar et al., 1999) and area occupied by it shows a 7% increase in the area of the OE it occupies in 21-day-old RTP1,2DKO (p=0.03 Mann Whitney U test, wild-type mean area 20%, ± 5 (SD), RTP1,2DKO mean area 27%, ± 6 (SD)) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis with statistical significance (p=0.03) shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No significant difference in the GAP43 positive layer is observed between RTP1,2DKO and their littermates at 1 day nor at 6 months.
source: No significant difference in the GAP43 positive layer is observed between RTP1,2DKO and their littermates at 1 day nor at 6 months (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Wild-type mice show robust EOG responses to all odorants at concentrations as low as 0.01%.
source: Wild-type mice show robust EOG responses to all odorants at concentrations as low as 0.01% (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by EOG data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: RTP1,2DKO mice showed striking deficits in their EOG response.
source: In contrast, RTP1,2DKO mice showed striking deficits in their response.
evidence: Supported by EOG data comparing wild-type and RTP1,2DKO responses.

claim: Responses to most odors in RTP1,2DKO were identical to the blank stimulus (air only).
source: Responses to most odors were identical to the blank stimulus (air only), although some sensitivity was maintained for a subset of odorants (2-heptanone, amyl acetate, isomenthone) compared to the wild-types (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Supported by EOG data shown in Figures 3B-C.

claim: Some sensitivity was maintained for a subset of odorants (2-heptanone, amyl acetate, isomenthone) in RTP1,2DKO compared to wild-types.
source: Responses to most odors were identical to the blank stimulus (air only), although some sensitivity was maintained for a subset of odorants (2-heptanone, amyl acetate, isomenthone) compared to the wild-types (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Supported by EOG data shown in Figures 3B-C.

claim: The reduction of mature OSNs and the loss of surface OR expression corresponds to a dramatic loss of odorant sensitivity in RTP1,2DKO.
source: Thus, the reduction of mature OSNs and the loss of surface OR expression corresponds to a dramatic loss of odorant sensitivity in RTP1,2DKO.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of reduced mature OSNs, lack of OR trafficking, and diminished EOG responses.

claim: 3.8% of all genes (926/24,661) were differentially expressed between RTP1,2DKO and wild-type.
source: Differential expression analysis comparing RTP1,2DKO to wild-type littermates revealed that 3.8% of all genes (926/24,661) were differentially expressed between the two genotypes, among which 805 were downregulated and 121 were upregulated in RTP1,2DKO (FDR corrected p<0.05, see Experimental Procedures for details).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq differential expression analysis with FDR corrected p<0.05.

claim: 805 genes were downregulated and 121 were upregulated in RTP1,2DKO.
source: Differential expression analysis comparing RTP1,2DKO to wild-type littermates revealed that 3.8% of all genes (926/24,661) were differentially expressed between the two genotypes, among which 805 were downregulated and 121 were upregulated in RTP1,2DKO (FDR corrected p<0.05, see Experimental Procedures for details).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq differential expression analysis with FDR corrected p<0.05.

claim: Canonical signaling molecules known to be expressed in mature OSNs including Gnal, Adcy3, and Cnga2 were less abundant in the RTP1,2DKO.
source: Canonical signaling molecules known to be expressed in mature OSNs including Gnal (Gαolf), Adcy3 (ACIII), and Cnga2 were less abundant in the RTP1,2DKO consistent with a reduced number of mature OSNs in absence of RTP1 and RTP2.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data and consistent with reduced mature OSN numbers.

claim: No significant difference was found in the expression levels of housekeeping genes like Gapdh and β actin.
source: We found no significant difference in the expression levels of housekeeping genes like Gapdh and β actin (Supplementary file 1) (Kouadjo et al., 2007), neither did we see any compensatory increase in other RTP family members Rtp3 or Rtp4.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: No compensatory increase in other RTP family members Rtp3 or Rtp4 was observed.
source: We found no significant difference in the expression levels of housekeeping genes like Gapdh and β actin (Supplementary file 1) (Kouadjo et al., 2007), neither did we see any compensatory increase in other RTP family members Rtp3 or Rtp4.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data.

claim: 62% of intact ORs (678/1088) were significantly affected by the loss of RTP1 and RTP2.
source: In a comparison between wild-type and RTP1,2DKO we found that 62% of intact ORs (678/1088) were significantly affected by the loss of RTP1 and RTP2 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Close to half of the annotated intact ORs (562/1088) were downregulated in RTP1,2DKO.
source: Close to half of the annotated intact ORs (562/1088) were downregulated in RTP1,2DKO (FDR corrected p<0.05), consistent with fewer OSNs in the mutant.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq analysis with FDR corrected p<0.05.

claim: A small subset of OR transcripts (116/1088) were upregulated in RTP1,2DKO mice.
source: Unexpectedly however, a small subset of OR transcripts (116/1088) were upregulated in RTP1,2DKO mice (FDR corrected p<0.05) (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1(A-B)).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq analysis with FDR corrected p<0.05 shown in Figure 4B and supplemental figures.

claim: 531/1088 ORs were underrepresented and 202/1088 were overrepresented when normalized using only reads mapped on intact ORs.
source: To remove any possible confounding variables from non-OSN cells, we normalized our read counts using only reads mapped on intact ORs and found that 531/1088 were underrepresented and 202/1088 were overrepresented (FDR corrected p<0.05) (Figure 4C,F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq analysis with OR-specific normalization and FDR corrected p<0.05.

claim: For all uORs tested, fewer OSNs were positive in RTP1,2DKO.
source: For all uORs tested, fewer OSNs were positive in RTP1,2DKO (Figure 4D–E) (p<0.05 Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: Supported by RNA in situ hybridization data with statistical significance (p<0.05) shown in Figures 4D-E.

claim: The frequencies for the tested oORs were greater in RTP1,2DKO.
source: In stark contrast, the frequencies for the tested oORs were greater in RTP1,2DKO (p<0.05, Mann-Whitney U test) (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: Supported by RNA in situ hybridization data with statistical significance (p<0.05) shown in Figures 4G-H.

claim: OR gene choice is biased in RTP1,2DKO towards a specific subset of receptor types.
source: These results demonstrate that OR gene choice is biased in RTP1,2DKO towards a specific subset of receptor types.
evidence: Inferred from the differential representation of uORs and oORs in RTP1,2DKO.

claim: oORs as a group are more abundantly expressed than uORs in the wild-type.
source: Curiously, we found that oORs as a group are more abundantly expressed than uORs in the wild-type.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq abundance data.

claim: OR genes that were not classified as either underrepresented nor overrepresented (NS) are expressed at significantly lower abundance levels than both oORs and uORs.
source: The OR genes that were not classified as either underrepresented nor overrepresented (NS, not significant) exhibited a wide range of changes in expression levels between the wild-type and RTP1,2DKO, but are expressed at significantly lower abundance levels than both oORs and uORs (Figure 4I) (p<0.0001 one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (p<0.0001, one-way ANOVA) shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Wild-type showed an increase for OSNs expressing the uORs tested both at 21 days and 6 months.
source: In the case of the uOR mix, wild-type showed an increase for OSNs expressing the uORs we tested both at 21 days and 6 months (Figure 5A–B) consistent to the increasing proportion of mature OSNs in the OE indicated by larger OMP and ACIII layers (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: Supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 5A-B.

claim: RTP1,2DKO showed no obvious increase in the fraction of cells expressing uORs with age.
source: However, RTP1,2DKO showed no obvious increase in the fraction of cells expressing these ORs with age, while on the other hand, in RTP1,2DKO the number of neurons expressing oORs showed a dramatic increase both from 1 day old to 21 days and from 21 days to 6 months (p<0.0001 one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test) (Figure 5C–D) demonstrating that the RTP1,2DKO OE is progressively populated by oORs.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis with statistical significance (p<0.0001) shown in Figures 5C-D.

claim: In RTP1,2DKO the number of neurons expressing oORs showed a dramatic increase both from 1 day old to 21 days and from 21 days to 6 months.
source: However, RTP1,2DKO showed no obvious increase in the fraction of cells expressing these ORs with age, while on the other hand, in RTP1,2DKO the number of neurons expressing oORs showed a dramatic increase both from 1 day old to 21 days and from 21 days to 6 months (p<0.0001 one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test) (Figure 5C–D) demonstrating that the RTP1,2DKO OE is progressively populated by oORs.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis with statistical significance (p<0.0001) shown in Figures 5C-D.

claim: The RTP1,2DKO OE is progressively populated by oORs.
source: However, RTP1,2DKO showed no obvious increase in the fraction of cells expressing these ORs with age, while on the other hand, in RTP1,2DKO the number of neurons expressing oORs showed a dramatic increase both from 1 day old to 21 days and from 21 days to 6 months (p<0.0001 one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test) (Figure 5C–D) demonstrating that the RTP1,2DKO OE is progressively populated by oORs.
evidence: Inferred from the dramatic increase in oOR-expressing neurons with age in RTP1,2DKO.

claim: Fewer Olfr151 expressing OSNs were present in RTP1,2DKO.
source: We saw that fewer Olfr151 expressing OSNs were present in RTP1,2DKO (p=0.0028, Mann-Whitney U test), as expected for a uOR.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis with statistical significance (p=0.0028).

claim: More β2AR positive OSNs were present in RTP1,2DKO compared with wild-type.
source: Strikingly, more β2AR positive OSNs were present in RTP1,2DKO compared with wild-type (p<0.001, Mann-Whitney U test) (Figure 6C–D), suggesting that it is the protein sequence and not the locus of the OR that determines whether a given OR is underrepresented or overrepresented.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis with statistical significance (p<0.001) shown in Figures 6C-D.

claim: It is the protein sequence and not the locus of the OR that determines whether a given OR is underrepresented or overrepresented.
source: Strikingly, more β2AR positive OSNs were present in RTP1,2DKO compared with wild-type (p<0.001, Mann-Whitney U test) (Figure 6C–D), suggesting that it is the protein sequence and not the locus of the OR that determines whether a given OR is underrepresented or overrepresented.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that β2AR expressed from the Olfr151 locus shows opposite behavior to Olfr151 in RTP1,2DKO.

claim: oORs as a group showed more OR surface expression than uORs in HEK293T cells.
source: oORs as a group showed more OR surface expression than uORs (p<0.05, Mann-Whitney U test) (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis with statistical significance (p<0.05) shown in Figures 6E-G.

claim: The ORs that show most robust cell surface expression were all oORs.
source: Notably, the ORs that show most robust cell surface expression were all oORs.
evidence: Supported by FACS data comparing uORs and oORs.

claim: RTP-independent trafficking of ORs may be related to increased frequencies of OSNs expressing oORs.
source: Even though trafficking mechanisms between OSNs and HEK293T cells are likely to be different, our data are consistent with the idea that RTP-independent trafficking of ORs may be related to increased frequencies of OSNs expressing oORs.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between surface expression in heterologous cells and overrepresentation in vivo.

claim: The number of OMP-positive OSNs expressing uORs show a 69% decrease in RTP1,2DKO.
source: We found that the number of immature OMP-negative OSNs expressing uORs are similar in RTP1,2DKO and het controls, whereas the number of OMP-positive OSNs expressing uORs show a 69% decrease in RTP1,2DKO. (p=0.024 Mann Whitney U test) (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis with statistical significance (p=0.024) shown in Figures 7B-D.

claim: The number of immature OMP-negative OSNs expressing uORs are similar in RTP1,2DKO and het controls.
source: We found that the number of immature OMP-negative OSNs expressing uORs are similar in RTP1,2DKO and het controls, whereas the number of OMP-positive OSNs expressing uORs show a 69% decrease in RTP1,2DKO. (p=0.024 Mann Whitney U test) (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figures 7B-D.

claim: OSNs expressing Olfr1395 in both het and RTP1,2DKO were activated to its cognate ligand TMT.
source: Using the induction of phospho ribosomal protein S6 (pS6), a marker for neuronal activation (Knight et al., 2012), we found that OSNs expressing Olfr1395 in both het and RTP1,2DKO were activated to its cognate ligand TMT (p<0.0001 one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc test) (Figure 7E,G).
evidence: Supported by pS6 induction data with statistical significance (p<0.0001) shown in Figures 7E and 7G.

claim: OSNs expressing Olfr923 in het, but not RTP1,2DKO were activated by their cognate ligand acetophenone.
source: In contrast OSNs expressing Olfr923 in het, but not RTP1,2DKO were activated by their cognate ligand acetophenone (Figure 7E–F).
evidence: Supported by pS6 induction data shown in Figures 7E-F.

claim: OSNs expressing oORs mature and function in the RTP1,2DKO.
source: These data show that OSNs expressing oORs mature and function in the RTP1,2DKO.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that oOR-expressing OSNs respond to cognate ligands in RTP1,2DKO.

claim: RTP1,2DKO mice have an increased number of OSNs undergoing cell death.
source: Immunostaining against active caspase 3, a cell death marker, suggested that RTP1,2DKO mice have an increased number of OSNs undergoing cell death (p<0.01, Mann-Whitney U test) (Cowan et al., 2001) (Figure 7H–I).
evidence: Supported by active caspase 3 immunostaining with statistical significance (p<0.01) shown in Figures 7H-I.

claim: More OSNs in immature and mature layers both undergo cell death in RTP1,2DKO.
source: Active caspase three staining in conjunction with OMP suggested that more OSNs in immature and mature layers both undergo cell death in RTP1,2DKO (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by double staining data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Immature OSNs in the OMP negative layer rarely undergo cell death in wild-type.
source: Notably, immature OSNs in the OMP negative layer rarely undergo cell death in wild-type (Figure 7J) (Jia et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by active caspase 3 staining data shown in Figure 7J and citation to Jia et al., 2010.

claim: OSNs expressing uORs are more likely to undergo cell death in RTP1,2DKO.
source: Together, these observations are consistent with the idea that OSNs expressing uORs are more likely to undergo cell death in RTP1,2DKO.
evidence: Inferred from the increased cell death and reduced mature uOR-expressing OSNs in RTP1,2DKO.

claim: There were more nATF5 positive OSNs in RTP1,2DKO mice.
source: Indeed, we observed that there were more nATF5 positive OSNs in RTP1,2DKO mice (p<0.001, Mann-Whitney U Test) and some of these OSNs were located closer to the apical surface, a phenomenon that was not observed in the wild-types, suggesting that nATF5 expression persists during the OSN development in RTP1,2DKO animals (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: Supported by nATF5 immunostaining with statistical significance (p<0.001) shown in Figures 8A-B.

claim: Some nATF5 positive OSNs in RTP1,2DKO were located closer to the apical surface, a phenomenon that was not observed in the wild-types.
source: Indeed, we observed that there were more nATF5 positive OSNs in RTP1,2DKO mice (p<0.001, Mann-Whitney U Test) and some of these OSNs were located closer to the apical surface, a phenomenon that was not observed in the wild-types, suggesting that nATF5 expression persists during the OSN development in RTP1,2DKO animals (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: Supported by nATF5 immunostaining data shown in Figures 8A-B.

claim: nATF5 expression persists during the OSN development in RTP1,2DKO animals.
source: Indeed, we observed that there were more nATF5 positive OSNs in RTP1,2DKO mice (p<0.001, Mann-Whitney U Test) and some of these OSNs were located closer to the apical surface, a phenomenon that was not observed in the wild-types, suggesting that nATF5 expression persists during the OSN development in RTP1,2DKO animals (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: Inferred from the expanded and apically-located nATF5 expression in RTP1,2DKO.

claim: Expanded expression was observed for LSD1 in RTP1,2DKO.
source: Similarly, expanded expression was observed for LSD1, a histone demethylase whose expression depends on nATF5 (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by LSD1 immunostaining data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The number of OSNs co-expressing Olfr151 and nATF5 was significantly higher in RTP1,2DKO than in the wild-type.
source: We observed that the number of OSNs co-expressing Olfr151 and nATF5 was significantly higher in RTP1,2DKO than in the wild-type (p<0.05, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis with statistical significance (p<0.05).

claim: The number of OSNs co-expressing β2AR and nATF5 in the β2AR:IRES:tauLacZ mouse was not different from the wild-type.
source: In contrast, the number of OSNs co-expressing β2AR and nATF5 in the β2AR:IRES:tauLacZ mouse was not different from the wild-type (p=1, Fisher's exact test)(Figure 8D–F).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis with statistical test (p=1) shown in Figures 8D-F.

claim: Delivery of ORs to the membrane plays a role in terminating the UPR.
source: As Olfr151 but not β2ARs require RTPs for surface expression, these data suggest that delivery of ORs to the membrane plays a role in terminating the UPR.
evidence: Inferred from the differential nATF5 colocalization between Olfr151 and β2AR in RTP1,2DKO.

claim: Higher numbers of OSNs expressing uORs colocalized with nATF5 in RTP1,2DKO as a group.
source: As expected, higher numbers of OSNs expressing uORs colocalized with nATF5 in RTP1,2DKO as a group (p=0.007, Mann-Whitney U test), whereas no significant difference was observed when oORs were tested (p=0.937, Mann-Whitney U test) (Figure 8G–H).
evidence: Supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry with statistical significance (p=0.007) shown in Figures 8G-H.

claim: No significant difference in nATF5 colocalization was observed when oORs were tested.
source: As expected, higher numbers of OSNs expressing uORs colocalized with nATF5 in RTP1,2DKO as a group (p=0.007, Mann-Whitney U test), whereas no significant difference was observed when oORs were tested (p=0.937, Mann-Whitney U test) (Figure 8G–H).
evidence: Supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry with statistical test (p=0.937) shown in Figures 8G-H.

claim: OSNs expressing uORs contribute to the expanded expression of nATF5 in RTP1,2DKO.
source: These observations suggest that OSNs expressing uORs contribute to the expanded expression of nATF5 in RTP1,2DKO and are further consistent with the idea that surface trafficking of ORs is linked to turning off UPR.
evidence: Inferred from the increased nATF5 colocalization with uORs but not oORs in RTP1,2DKO.

claim: Surface trafficking of ORs is linked to turning off UPR.
source: These observations suggest that OSNs expressing uORs contribute to the expanded expression of nATF5 in RTP1,2DKO and are further consistent with the idea that surface trafficking of ORs is linked to turning off UPR.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between OR trafficking capability and nATF5 expression.

claim: Only 17% of tdTomato positive cells from RTP1,2DKO OE also express Olfr151 in comparison to 31% OSNs from the wild-type.
source: We found that only 17% of tdTomato positive cells from RTP1,2DKO OE (n = 24/140 neurons) also express Olfr151 in comparison to 31% OSNs from the wild-type (n = 79/258 neurons) (p<0.05, Fisher's exact test) and 38% (n = 66/172 neurons) in the heterozygotes (p<0.05, Fisher's exact test) (Figure 9B–C).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing analysis with statistical significance (p<0.05) shown in Figures 9B-C.

claim: The loss of RTPs leads to the frequent termination of Olfr151 gene expression.
source: This suggests that the loss of RTPs leads to the frequent termination of Olfr151 gene expression.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced proportion of tdTomato+/Olfr151+ double positive cells in RTP1,2DKO.

claim: No Olfr143 and tdTomato double positive OSNs were found in both RTP1,2DKO or their wild-type littermates.
source: We found no Olfr143 and tdTomato double positive OSNs in both RTP1,2DKO or their wild-type littermates, indicating that there is no higher likelihood of the gene switching between these ORs.
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis data.

claim: There is no higher likelihood of the gene switching between Olfr151 and Olfr143.
source: We found no Olfr143 and tdTomato double positive OSNs in both RTP1,2DKO or their wild-type littermates, indicating that there is no higher likelihood of the gene switching between these ORs.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of Olfr143/tdTomato double positive cells.

claim: Olfactory axons entered the OB and innervate to the glomerular layer in RTP1,2DKO.
source: Olfactory axons entered the OB and innervate to the glomerular layer based on our OMP immunostaining in RTP1,2DKO (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by OMP immunostaining data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Olfr151 expressing OSNs were unable to converge in the OB in RTP1,2DKO.
source: However, using M71-IRES-tau GFP mice we found that Olfr151 expressing OSNs were unable to converge in the OB in RTP1,2DKO while their wild-type littermates had two Olfr151 glomeruli in each of their OBs as expected (Figure 10B–C).
evidence: Supported by GFP fluorescence data shown in Figures 10B-C.

claim: Wild-type littermates had two Olfr151 glomeruli in each of their OBs.
source: However, using M71-IRES-tau GFP mice we found that Olfr151 expressing OSNs were unable to converge in the OB in RTP1,2DKO while their wild-type littermates had two Olfr151 glomeruli in each of their OBs as expected (Figure 10B–C).
evidence: Supported by GFP fluorescence data shown in Figures 10B-C.

claim: Both the wild-type and RTP1,2DKO mice formed β2AR glomeruli.
source: Both the wild-type and RTP1,2DKO mice formed glomeruli, however the mutant mice had ectopic glomeruli for OSNs expressing this GPCR (Figure 10B–C).
evidence: Supported by LacZ staining data shown in Figures 10B-C.

claim: The mutant mice had ectopic glomeruli for OSNs expressing β2AR.
source: Both the wild-type and RTP1,2DKO mice formed glomeruli, however the mutant mice had ectopic glomeruli for OSNs expressing this GPCR (Figure 10B–C).
evidence: Supported by LacZ staining data shown in Figures 10B-C.

claim: The RTP1,2DKO mice do not have a complete set of glomeruli, but retain the ability to form them.
source: These data suggest the RTP1,2DKO mice do not have a complete set of glomeruli, but retain the ability to form them.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of Olfr151 glomeruli but presence of β2AR glomeruli in RTP1,2DKO.

claim: tdTomato-positive axons formed small glomeruli in RTP1,2DKO;M71-IRES-cre; Rosa26-lox-stop-lox-tdTomato mice.
source: We observed tdTomato-positive axons forming small glomeruli in RTP1,2DKO;M71-IRES-cre; Rosa26-lox-stop-lox-tdTomato mice (2 out of 3 mice examined had 1 glomerulus each)(Figure 10B–C).
evidence: Supported by tdTomato fluorescence data shown in Figures 10B-C.

claim: OSNs initially expressing Olfr151 may switch and/or stabilize expression of a specific OR, presumably an oOR, and axons from these OSNs can converge in the OB.
source: This may indicate that OSNs initially expressing Olfr151 switch and/or stabilize expression of a specific OR, presumably an oOR, and axons from these OSNs can converge in the OB.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation of tdTomato-positive glomeruli in RTP1,2DKO.

claim: The absence of RTP1 and RTP2 leads to the underrepresentation of nearly half of the ORs, while about 10% of the ORs are significantly overrepresented.
source: The absence of RTP1 and RTP2 leads to the underrepresentation of nearly half of the ORs, while about 10% of the ORs are significantly overrepresented.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data showing differential OR representation.

claim: Protein sequences of ORs differentially influence OR gene choice, which is linked to trafficking of ORs to the cell surface.
source: Our data indicate that protein sequences of ORs differentially influence OR gene choice, which is linked to trafficking of ORs to the cell surface.
evidence: Inferred from the β2AR experiment and differential surface expression of uORs vs oORs.

claim: The RTPs suppress UPR response by allowing ORs to exit the ER and be transported to the plasma membrane.
source: In our model, the RTPs suppress UPR response by allowing ORs to exit the ER and be transported to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental observations.

claim: uORs are not trafficked to the cell surface in the absence of the RTPs, giving rise to persistent UPR in the OSNs that express them.
source: uORs are not trafficked to the cell surface in the absence of the RTPs, giving rise to persistent UPR in the OSNs that express them; as a consequence, destabilization of the initial OR gene choice leads to cell death or to the stabilization of another OR.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on experimental observations.

claim: Destabilization of the initial OR gene choice leads to cell death or to the stabilization of another OR.
source: uORs are not trafficked to the cell surface in the absence of the RTPs, giving rise to persistent UPR in the OSNs that express them; as a consequence, destabilization of the initial OR gene choice leads to cell death or to the stabilization of another OR.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on experimental observations.

claim: oORs are trafficked to the cell surface as functional proteins in the absence of the RTPs, allowing these OSNs to terminate UPR and stabilize gene expression.
source: In contrast, oORs are trafficked to the cell surface as functional proteins in the absence of the RTPs, allowing these OSNs to terminate UPR and stabilize gene expression.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on experimental observations.

claim: RTP1,2DKO mice had diminished but not abolished responses to odorants.
source: Our data suggest that mice without RTP1 and RTP2 had diminished but not abolished responses to odorants.
evidence: Supported by EOG data showing residual responses to some odorants.

claim: OSNs expressing oORs are likely to mature and be functional in RTP1,2DKO.
source: Our data show that OSNs expressing oORs are likely to mature and be functional in RTP1,2DKO, explaining the residual responses observed in the mutant.
evidence: Inferred from the functional responses of oOR-expressing OSNs and their maturation.

claim: oOR-expressing OSNs become more abundant in the mutant OE as the mouse ages.
source: These OSNs become more abundant in the mutant OE as the mouse ages indicating that these ORs help maintain the olfactory ability of these mice.
evidence: Supported by age-dependent increase in oOR-expressing OSNs shown in Figure 5.

claim: oORs help maintain the olfactory ability of RTP1,2DKO mice.
source: These OSNs become more abundant in the mutant OE as the mouse ages indicating that these ORs help maintain the olfactory ability of these mice.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between oOR abundance and residual olfactory function.

claim: Olfr78 (MOR18-2) and its human ortholog OR51E2 have been reported to function in the prostate, airway and kidney as well as the carotid body.
source: One well-established example of a functional OR outside the olfactory system is Olfr78 (also known as MOR18-2) and its human ortholog OR51E2, which have been reported to function in the prostate, airway and kidney as well as the carotid body (Aisenberg et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2006; Pluznick et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Aisenberg et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2006; Pluznick et al., 2013).

claim: Olfr78 is an oOR and is trafficked to the cell surface in heterologous cells without the RTPs.
source: This receptor is an oOR and is trafficked to the cell surface in heterologous cells without the RTPs (Zhou et al., 2016; Pluznick et al., 2011; Neuhaus et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations (Zhou et al., 2016; Pluznick et al., 2011; Neuhaus et al., 2009).

claim: ORs expressed in the bladder and thyroid (Olfr544, Olfr558, and Olfr1386) are all oORs.
source: It is also interesting to note that ORs expressed in the bladder and thyroid (Olfr544, Olfr558, and Olfr1386) are all oORs (Kang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kang et al., 2015.

claim: oORs expressed outside the OE are more likely to play chemosensory roles.
source: Together, it is tempting to speculate that oORs expressed outside the OE are more likely to play chemosensory roles (Feingold et al., 1999).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that known functional ORs outside the OE are oORs.
